The wobble hypothesis explains the degeneracy of the genetic code.
The wobble hypothesis states that codon-anticodon pairing follows the traditional Watson—Crick
tules (G pairs with C and A pairs with U) for the first two bases of the codon but can be less
stringent for the third/last base. It has been observed that a tRNA can recognize more than one
codon for a specific amino acid, especially in the last nucleotide of the codon triplet. This is
referred to as degeneracy and its mechanism can be explained by the wobble hypothesis.
The first base of the anticodon moves to permit nontraditional pairing with the last base of the
codon. This movement is called wobble and is possible because the first base of the anticodon is
not as spatially defined as the other two bases. Due to the wobbling, 61 tRNA species are not
required to read the 61 codons.
For example, three codons for glycine—GGU, GGC, and GGA—can form a base pair from one
anticodon, 3’ CCI 5’ ie, I, inosine, can base pair with U, C, and A, as shown in the diagram below.
Other options:
Option A: The genetic code is universal because it is the same for all living organisms.
Option B: The genetic code is unambiguous because each codon is specific for only one amino
acid. Example: GGA only codes for Glycine.
Option D: The genetic code is non-punctuated. This means that once the reading commences at a
specific start codon, it is continuous and is read continuously as triplets until a stop codon is
reached without stopping.

The correct sequence of events for PCR among the given options is denaturation, annealing, and
extension.
The process of PCR is as follows:
The DNA sample is first heat-denatured at >90°C (90-96 degrees Celsius for 3 minutes) to
separate the two strands of the template DNA containing the target sequence; the primers (which
attach to the 3' end of the flanking sequence) are added in excess, are allowed to anneal to the
DNA (typically at 50-75°C) in order to generate the required template-primer hybridization
complex. Under suitable conditions and presence of deoxynucleotides, elongation of the DNA
stand occurs.
The number of copies produced in the presence of an unlimited supply of deoxynucleotides and
enzymes is given by - 2 to the power n (where n is the number of PCR cycles)
* 20 cycles provide an amplification of 220 = 106 or 1 million copies
* 30 cycles provides an amplification of 230 =109 or 1 billion copies

Each single motor neuron and the muscle fibers it innervates constitute a motor unit.
¢ The number of muscle fibers in a motor unit varies.
¢ In muscles concerned with fine, graded, precise movement, (eg. extraoccular muscles) each
motor unit innervates very few (three to six) muscle fibers.

be upto 600.

in a motor unit are of the same type.
* On the basis of the type of muscle fiber they innervate, and thus on the basis of the duration of
their twitch contraction, motor units are divided into S (slow), FR (fast, resistant to fatigue), and
FF (fast, fatigable) units.

Excitation contraction coupling refers to the process by which the membrane depolarization of the
muscle fibre (excitation) leads to the contraction of the muscle.
The steps of excitation-contraction coupling in skeletal muscle are as follows:
* Motor-neuron discharge causes the release of acetylcholine at the motor endplate, which binds
to the nicotinic acetylcholine receptors.
¢ This causes increased Na+ and K+ conductance in the endplate membrane, leading to the
generation of end-plate potential, which is a local potential.
* When the local endplate potential reaches a threshold for the muscle fibre, and an action
potential is generated.
+ The generated action potential passes inward through the T tubules, leading to the spread of
depolarisation.
* The depolarization of the muscle fibre causes the release of Ca2+ from terminal cisterns of
sarcoplasmic reticulum and diffusion to thick and thin filaments.

+ The calcium released, binds to troponin C, uncovering myosin-binding sites on actin.
+ The formation of cross-linkages between actin and myosin and sliding of thin on thick filaments
causes contraction of the skeletal muscle.
Steps in relaxation:
+ The cytoplasmic calcium is pumped back into the sarcoplasmic reticulum, by the action of
SERCA (sarcoplasmic endoplasmic reticulum calcium ATPase).
¢ Once the calcium concentration is lowered, the interaction between actin and myosin ceases, and
the muscle relaxes.
Other options:
Statement 1: Incorrect - Extracellular calcium levels play an important role in muscle contraction.
When there is a decrease in extracellular calcium as in hypocalcemia, the voltage-gated sodium
channels are activated, which causes sodium influx. The increased intraeellular sodium
concentration causes sustained depolarization, which.may lead to tetariy.
Statement 2: Incorrect - Ca2+ is not released from mtitochondriasIt is released from the
sarcoplasmic reticulum. ‘. ‘. ,
Statement 4: Voltage-gated calcium channels on T-tubules (part of sareolemma) are activated by a
depolarizing stimulus, which causeg-the release of calcium from the sarcoplasmic reticulum. The
increased calcium concentration ‘will eventually lead to muscle‘contraction.

The length of the muscle fiber at the onset of contraction which is required to attain
maximum active tension is known as resting length.
Resting length is also known as the optimum length. It is about 2um. At this length, there is
a maximal overlap between the actin and myosin fibers and therefore, the maximum number of
cross-bridge binding sites are formed.

Passive tension is the tension in a muscle when it is not stimulated. Total tension is the tension
developed when a muscle contracts isometrically in response to a maximal stimulus.
Active tension = Total tension - Passive tension

cross-bridges between the actin and myosin fibers. Hence, at the resting length, maximum active
tension is produced and the muscle fiber contracts with a maximum force of contraction.

Gibbs-Donnan equilibrium explains the effect of a non-diffusible ion on the distribution of permeant ions.
Consider the situation depicted below.
The membrane is permeable to K+ and Cl-. However, it is impermeable to the proteins. The impermeable protein molecules hinder the movement of K+ (negative charge of the proteins holding back positive charge of K+) and favor the movement of Cl- (like charges repel).
According to the Gibbs-Donnan equation, at equilibrium, the concentration ratios of diffusible ions are equal across the membrane:
[K+]x / [K+]y = [Cl-]y / [Cl-]x
Cross-multiplying:
[K+]x[Cl-]x = [K+]y[Cl-]y

Oxygen diffuses from alveoli to blood along the concentration gradient i.e. passive process (ATP is not used).

It diffuses across respiratory membrane.

It is governed by Fick's law of diffusion:
D ∝ (ΔP × A × S) / (d × √MW)

Where:
• D is the diffusion rate
• ΔP is the partial pressure difference between the two ends of the diffusion pathway
• A is the cross-sectional area of the pathway
• S is the solubility of the gas
• d is the distance of diffusion
• MW is the molecular weight of the gas

Diffusion coefficient of the gas is proportional to S/√MW.

The elastic recoil of the elastic arteries helps in continuous blood flow.

The large elastic arteries distend and recoil during systole and diastole respectively due to abundant elastic tissue. The recoiling acts as an additional force that pushes blood into smaller arteries. So, blood flows continuously through arteries but with some fluctuation in pressure during systole and diastole.

The main differences between the elastic and muscular arteries are shown in the table given below:

Structure | Elastic artery | Muscular artery
Tunica intima | The internal elastic lamina cannot be distinguished from the surrounding tunica media | The internal elastic lamina is distinct
Tunica media | Predominantly of elastic fibers. Few smooth muscle cells. | Predominantly of smooth muscle cells. Very few elastic fibers.
Tunica adventitia | Relatively thin and consists mainly of elastic fibers | Relatively thicker and consists of fibroblastic tissue.

Other options:

Option A: The elastic arteries are also known as conducting vessels, as their main function is to conduct the blood from the heart, whereas the muscular arteries are known as distributing vessels.

Option B: The internal elastic lamina in the elastic arteries is not distinct and cannot be differentiated from the tunica media as the structure of the internal elastic lamina is same as that of the elastic fibers present in tunica media of elastic arteries.

Option C: The tunica media of the elastic arteries is predominantly made up of elastic tissue. Between the elastic membranes, there is some loose connective tissue. Some smooth muscle cells may be present.

1% of cellular DNA is in mitochondria.

Human mitochondria contain 2 to 10 copies of a small circular ~16 kbp (kilo base pair) dsDNA molecule that makes up approximately 1% of total cellular DNA. Out of 37 genes in human mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA), 22 genes code for transfer RNAs, 2 for ribosomal RNAs, and 13 for proteins that play key roles in the respiratory chain. A feature unique to human mitochondrial mtDNA is maternal non-mendelian inheritance because all mitochondria are contributed by the ovum during zygote formation. Thus, mothers transmit mtDNA to all their offspring.

Normal plasma osmolarity (~290 mOsm/L) is mainly due to Na+ and its accompanying anions, principally Cl− and HCO3−.

• Osmolarity (mOsm/L) = 2 [Na+] (mEq/L) + 0.055 [glucose] (mg/dL) + 0.36 [BUN] (mg/dL)
• Because sodium and its associated anions (Cl−, HCO3−) account for about 94 per cent of the solute in the extracellular compartment, plasma osmolarity (Posm) can be roughly approximated as:
• Posm = 2.1 × Plasma sodium concentration
• With a plasma sodium concentration of 142 mEq/L, the plasma osmolarity would be estimated from the formula above to be about 298 mOsm/L.
• In conditions associated with renal disease, the contribution of two other solutes, glucose and urea, should be included.
• Because urea easily permeates most cell membranes, it exerts little effective osmotic pressure under steady-state conditions. (Ineffective osmoles)
• Contribution to plasma osmolarity:
• Na+ and associated anions: 270 mOsm/L
• Glucose: 5 mOsm/L
• Urea: 5 mOsm/L
• Plasma proteins: 2 mOsm/L
• Other ions: 8 mOsm/L

candidates.value:
Glutamate is a major excitatory neurotransmitter responsible for ~75% excitatory neurotransmission in the CNS.

Glutamate is the best-known example of excitatory amino acid neurotransmitters. It brings about its action via both ionotropic and metabotropic receptors.

Glutamate Receptors:

Ionotropic Glutamate Receptors
AMPA, Kainate receptors: Primarily permits influx of Na+ and efflux of K+ → EPSP (excitatory postsynaptic potential).
NMDA receptors: Permits ↑ influx of Ca2+ along with Na+ → EPSP (excitatory postsynaptic potential). Glycine binding to the NMDA receptor is essential for the receptor to respond to glutamate.

Metabotropic Glutamate Receptor (mGluR): Leads to either ↑ in IP3/DAG or ↓ cAMP.

candidates.value:
The distance of two-point discrimination is greatest at the back of the scapula.

The relative tactile acuity of a given region can be determined by the two-point discrimination test. Here, calipers are used to determine the minimum distance between the two points which can be perceived as two points. Greater the density of receptors → Smaller the receptive field → More precise the localization.
For e.g., Stimulus points on the back, for instance, must be separated by at least 65 mm before they can be distinguished as separate, whereas on the fingertips two stimuli are recognized if they are separated by as little as 2 mm. The lips have the greatest acuity (two-point discrimination threshold ~ 1 mm).
Clinical significance:
Blind individuals benefit from the tactile acuity of fingertips to facilitate the ability to read Braille. The dots forming Braille symbols are separated by 2.5 mm.
Two-point discrimination is used to test the integrity of the dorsal column (medial lemniscus) system.

candidates.value:
The percentage of cardiac output that bypasses the pulmonary circulation or physiological shunt is 2%. The fraction of mixed venous blood that does not become oxygenated as it moves from the right atrium to the left ventricle is called physiologic shunt.

Causes of physiological shunt:
• Extrapulmonary R→L anatomic shunt (normally ~1% of cardiac output)
• Intrapulmonary “true” shunt
• Flow past unventilated or collapsed alveoli (e.g., due to edema, pneumonia, atelectasis)
• Anatomic arterio-venous pathways: mixing of unoxygenated blood in bronchial veins with oxygenated blood in pulmonary capillaries or vein reduces the final partial pressure of O2 in the arterial blood (PaO2)
• Intrapulmonary regions with low ventilation/perfusion ratio: alveolar ventilation is not zero, but blood is not completely oxygenated (a virtual shunt, not a “true” shunt).

suspectLines.text: • Extrapulmonary R→L anatomic shunt (normally ~1% of cardiac output)

Decreased ventilation-perfusion ratio implies decreased oxygenation due to decreased ventilation with respect to perfusion. Hence, PAO2 decreases and PCO2 increases.

A decrease in the ventilation-perfusion ratio (VA/Q) is depicted by moving to the left along the normal ventilation-perfusion line as shown in the figure.

• Zone 1: lowest ventilation compared to Zones 2 and 3, but V >> Q, hence V/Q is high.
• PAO2 is highest.
• PACO2 is lowest.
• Zone 2: Ventilation almost equal to perfusion, but slightly lower, so V/Q is average (~0.8).
• Zone 3: highest ventilation compared to Zones 2 and 1, but Q >> V, hence V/Q is low.
• PAO2 is lowest.
• PACO2 is highest.

PAO2 = Alveolar partial pressure of oxygen.
PACO2 = Alveolar partial pressure of CO2.

candidates.subject: Physiology
candidates.value:
Equilibrium potential for an ion is calculated using the Nernst equation.
When there is a concentration gradient for an ion across the membrane, the ion tends to diffuse down the concentration gradient. The electric potential that exactly opposes this net diffusion is called the equilibrium potential for that ion. This is calculated using the Nernst equation.
It is expressed as the potential inside the cell (intracellular potential relative to the extracellular potential).
To calculate the value of the equilibrium potential:
Nernst equation
EMF (millivolts) = ±(61/z) × log(Concentration inside / Concentration outside)
Note: In this formula, the choice of concentration of the ion placed in the numerator and denominator does not matter because the formula is only used to derive the numerical value and not the sign (+/-). Mathematically, log(100/10) = 1 and log(10/100) = -1. Hence, changing the numerator and denominator only changes the sign and the numerical value remains the same.
This equation is used only to derive the numerical value of the potential. It is NOT used to derive the sign/charge (+/-).
The sign/charge is derived from logic:
• In a positive (+) ion, if the concentration of the + ion is greater outside, then the + ion moves from outside to inside. The intracellular potential becomes more positive relatively. Hence, the potential will be positive.
• In a positive (+) ion, if the concentration of the + ion is greater inside, then the + ion moves from inside to outside. The intracellular potential becomes more negative relatively (as + ion moves outside). Hence the potential will be negative.
• In a negative (-) ion, if the concentration of the - ion is greater outside, then the - ion moves from outside to inside. The intracellular potential becomes more negative relatively. Hence the potential will be negative.
• In a negative (-) ion, if the concentration of the - ion is greater inside, then the - ion moves from inside to outside. The intracellular potential becomes more positive relatively (as - ion moves outside). Hence the potential will be positive.

The potential of a positive ion across the membrane using Nernst equation is +60 mV.
EMF (millivolts) = ±(61/z) × log(Concentration inside / Concentration outside)
where z is the valency.
Deriving the numerical value:
EMF = (61/1) × log(10/100), giving a numerical value of 61 mV.
The choice of concentration of the ion placed in the numerator and denominator does not matter because the formula is only used to derive the numerical value and not the sign (+/-). Mathematically, log(100/10) = 1 and log(10/100) = -1. Hence, changing the numerator and denominator only changes the sign and the numerical value remains the same.
Deciding the sign/charge: a positive ion with greater concentration extracellularly will try to diffuse inside the cell. A positive intracellular potential is required to prevent this. Hence, the sign/charge (potential) is positive.
Hence, the potential across the membrane using the Nernst equation is +60 mV (the closest answer chosen).

candidates.subject: Physiology
candidates.value:
Forward digit span test is the best test among the given options.

Memory is of 3 types:
• Immediate
• Recent
• Remote

Immediate memory is attention dependent. Tests of attention and memory include
• Digit span test: Most important and best test for immediate memory
• Serial (100-7) subtraction test is the best for concentration
• Days of the week backwards
• Spell WORLD backwards
• (20–3) test

Digit span test

The examiner recites numbers randomly without any sequence and asks the patient to repeat the same. The examiner starts with a 2-number sequence and the digit span increases from 2 numbers to 3 numbers and so on. The patient is asked to repeat until he/she fails to repeat all numbers correctly.

Digit forward
• Normally a person can repeat up to 7 digits (+/- 2).
• E.g., Examiner says 2 - 4 - 8 - 1 - 5 - 7 - 9. The person has to repeat in the same order 2 - 4 - 8 - 1 - 5 - 7 - 9.

Digit backward
• Reproduction of longer digits in backward direction.
• Normally a person can repeat up to 5 digits (+/- 1) in backward direction (making option C wrong).
• Eg: Examiner says 2 - 4 - 8 - 1 - 5 - 7 - 9. The person has to repeat it backwards. 9 - 7 - 5 - 1 - 8 - 4 - 2.

Serial (100-7) subtraction test
• 5 scores / steps are taken in to account.
• 1st score – When the patient tells 93 (100 - 7 = 93).
• 2nd score - When the patient tells 86 (93 – 7 = 86).
• And so on . . 100 , 93 , 86 , 79 , 72 , 65.

Hence among the given options:

Digit span forward up to 7 digits with 2 skips allowed would be the answer of choice as it is the best test for immediate memory.

suspectLines.text: • Normally a person can repeat up to 7 digits (+/- 2).
• Normally a person can repeat up to 5 digits (+/- 1) in backward direction (making option C wrong).

candidates.value:
The relationship between the flow in a long narrow tube, the viscosity of the fluid, and the radius of the tube is expressed mathematically by Poiseuille's law.

Poiseuille-Hagen formula:
F = (PA − PB) × (π/8) × (1/η) × (1/L) × r⁴

Where F = flow; PA − PB = pressure difference between two ends of the tube; η = viscosity; r = radius; L = length.

candidates.value:
The percentage of cytosine in DNA will be 22%.

According to Chargaff's rule in cellular DNA, regardless of species:
A = T and G = C.
Purines = Pyrimidines, i.e. A + G = C + T.

In the question it is given that thymine is 28%, therefore adenine is also 28%. So, adenine + thymine = 56% and guanine + cytosine = 44%. Since guanine = cytosine, the percentage of cytosine = 44/2 = 22%.
